vignette:
Imani presents as a poised, articulate young woman, her nurse’s uniform always immaculate, her posture conveying a calm competence that belies the persistent tremor in her hands. She speaks of her life in two distinct parts: before the shelling, and after.

Before, life in her hometown was vibrant. She was a promising nursing student, navigating the familiar chaos of the local market for her mother, her days filled with the scent of spices and the warmth of a sun she took for granted. Her world was mapped by familiar landmarks: the university, the corner café, the ancient church whose bells marked the hours. Her future felt as solid and real as the cobblestones under her feet. She planned to work in the local clinic alongside her aunt.

The “after” began on a Tuesday. The first explosion wasn't a sound so much as a pressure change, a sudden, violent punch to the air that rattled the windows of her family’s apartment. The life she knew fractured in that instant. The next few days were a blur of running, of hiding in a cramped basement with neighbors, the world reduced to the smell of dust and fear and the rhythmic, terrifying thud of artillery. The memory that surfaces most often, unbidden and sharp, is not of the loudest explosion, but of the silence that followed. It was during a brief, desperate run for water that she saw the marketplace. It was gone. In its place was a crater of splintered wood, overturned carts, and a shocking, impossible stillness. The bright red of spilled tomatoes was everywhere, a sight so mundane yet so horrific it seared itself into her mind.

She and her younger brother eventually made it out, part of a tide of displaced people that carried them across a border and, eventually, through a resettlement program, to the United States. She threw herself into finishing her nursing certification. It was something tangible, a skill that made sense when nothing else did. She met her partner, David, a kind, steady software engineer who knows only the broad strokes of her past. He sees her strength, her resilience. He doesn’t see the nights she spends sitting on the edge of the bed, wide awake, listening to the house settle, convinced every creak is a footstep.

At work, Imani is a ghost in scrubs. She moves through the controlled chaos of the emergency department with a practiced efficiency. She can triage a multi-car pileup, insert an IV into a rolling vein, and speak to a frightened family with a soothing authority that feels like a costume she puts on at the start of her shift. But the hospital is a minefield. A gurney clattering down the hall sounds like a cart being overturned. The sharp smell of antiseptic can transport her back to a makeshift aid station. Last week, a resident dropped a metal tray in the cafeteria, and Imani flinched so violently she spilled coffee all over her front, her heart hammering against her ribs as if trying to escape her body. She spent the rest of her break locked in a bathroom stall, shaking.

With David, the disconnect is profound. He tries to be close, to understand. He’ll suggest they go to a Fourth of July celebration, and she will invent a reason to work, unable to explain that the thought of fireworks makes her physically ill. He’ll reach for her in the night, a gesture of simple affection, and she will flinch, her body rigid with a fear that has nothing to do with him. She feels a constant, gnawing guilt. Why her? Why did she get to build this new life when so many others, people she’d known since childhood, were reduced to dust in a marketplace? The question leaves her feeling hollow, detached from the love David offers, from the patients she cares for, from the very life she fought so hard to save. She often finds herself standing at her apartment window, watching the peaceful, orderly flow of traffic below, feeling as if she’s watching a film of someone else’s life.
